utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could I first ask the parties whether further discussions have led to any further agreement on the statement of Witness 144.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have not had any further discussions on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you intend to have any further discussions or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: From our perspective, we had those discussions yesterday in the last break and we disagreed on a fundamental matter and we didn't intend to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber will give a decision soon. It will an oral decision, I take it, that it will be given after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So Your Honour is not giving -- Your Honours are not giving a decision now in relation to the objections?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not right away. You would say that if we finish the cross-examination of the witness, we'd rather need a decision anyhow before we excuse the witness. That's, of course, something to be considered. If you think that for your cross-examination it would be important to have that decision, then we could --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In fact, it is, Your Honour, because there are some matters that I've objected to that if they are part of the evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's different, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- I'll have to cross-examine on them, so it will affect my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that it will take us any more than ten minutes to deliver that decision, but of course we first wanted to know whether any further agreement between the parties was there. So we'll adjourn for some ten minutes, and perhaps we could use that break that when we restart, that the witness is already in, because that means curtains down and to be pulled up again. We'll adjourn for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 2.25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber took a bit more than ten minutes. As far as your objections are concerned, Ms. Loukas, the Chamber would not accept in evidence paragraphs 20 and 21 of the statement. It does, however, admit into evidence paragraphs 22 - 23 was already out - 24, and in respect of 24, the Chamber notes that the relevance of that paragraph is mainly that the witness heard similar language in Kotor Varos as he heard from Belgrade. Then the objections up until 46 are further denied, so we admit all those paragraphs in evidence. Then we come to paragraph 60. We do not admit into evidence the last half-sentence of paragraph 60, starting with "but it was a step forward." At the same time, if the Prosecution would like to ask further questions about this issue, then it will have an opportunity to do so. As far as the first part of that sentence is concerned, starting with "the proclamation," the Chamber considers this to reflect the perception of the legal status of that proclamation by the witness. And of course, further questions can be put to the witness in that respect. Paragraph 63. The part starting with "ballot papers" is admitted into evidence, but not the subsequent sentence, starting with the word "this" and ending with the word "discrimination." In respect of paragraphs 66 and 67, the Chamber understands that in these paragraphs the witness puts into a certain context an experience he had himself. And paragraph 67 allows the Chamber to see whether the description of the event that is put in the same context by the witness is described in such a way that it is in accordance with evidence already presented, and to that extent, allows the Chamber to further assess reliability of the written statement. And therefore, 66 and 67 are admitted in evidence. Paragraph 90, the objection is also denied, Ms. Loukas. The Chamber considers paragraph 90 to reflect what kind of information, what information the witness received through the media, which, of course, does not automatically mean that whatever was shown on the media was the truth or was the complete truth or part of the truth, but at least it indicates what information could be received. That's the decision on your objections. Oh, no. We still have 99. 99, your objection is also denied. The Chamber understands, especially the first few lines of paragraph 99, to reflect the perception of the witness of what happened. So if it reads: "The statement by the JNA officers could not go unnoticed and it meant something like," then of course it does not -- admission into evidence does not mean that the Chamber shares the view that this was the meaning but that the Chamber accepts that this was the way the witness perceived that event. I think I dealt with all your objections, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All the objections have been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If this decision would cause the Prosecution to ask further questions about those parts that were not admitted, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will not need to ask any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Ms. Loukas, you may cross-examine the witness. Witness 144, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas, who is counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to my commencing, Your Honour, I might indicate that in light of the ruling on the objections, I may take a little bit longer than an hour. I still propose, as much as possible, to keep it within the hour, but I might take a little bit longer in view of the further matters that I'll have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if the witness might be shown the Defence document that has been I think given to the Prosecution and the interpreters and the registrar. Now, Witness, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D29.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I might indicate for the benefit of the Court, Your Honour, that this document was provisionally translated by Ms. Cmeric overnight, so the -- there's no actual official translation of the document in question. What I propose to do, in view of the fact that the interpreters do have the relevant document, if the witness might read the relevant portion that we have there onto the record, slowly, and then it can be placed on the record in that fashion and the interpretation can Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond come through at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do it the way you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have that document before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you would care to read slowly onto the record what's contained there in B/C/S. That's pages 220. There's a half page there, and half page on 221. And then I'll ask you some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We may make a practical suggestion. Ms. Cmeric is more familiar with this document and the court process, and the same objective would be achieved, I think, if she read this into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whoever reads it is, of course, the most important thing is that it's on the record, and perhaps Ms. Cmeric may have a better ability to know whether she is going too slow or too quick for the interpreters. Could you please -- would you mind, Ms. Loukas, to ask Ms. Cmeric --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I mean, that's a sensible solution. I thought it would be useful for the witness to actually read it himself, but I think the same purpose is served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's read out, could you also follow it by reading the text, and Ms. Cmeric will read it aloud. Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] On the 7th and 8th of February, 1992, in the village of Mehurici, near Travnik, a session of a military council was held that was later to be called an historical one. At this session, the commanders of the regional staffs and part of the Main Staff of the Patriotic League of Bosnia and Herzegovina met. The aim of this counselling was to harmonise plans by regions and the handing out of tasks for the following period of time. The preparation of this meeting began in late 1991, when I sent instructions to all the staffs in the fields, tasks for the RVS. This was a document that, among other things, paved the way for our local purpose industry. When we met, I presented the military and political situation at the meeting, and I presented an evaluation of our future strategy. The foundations of my presentation were agreed to and adopted at the meeting and put forward briefly in the first two items or paragraphs of the most important PL document. The directives for the defence of the sovereignty of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the presentation and reports of commanders, an immediate exchange of opinions and information, supplemented this document that was completed on the 25th of February in Sarajevo. As the document was being prepared and produced, as well as at the meeting in Mehurici itself, Rifat Bilajac and Zicro Suljevic assisted me as advisors. However, this directive is my own work. Copies were made of the handwritten document, and it was only typed up later and forwarded to the commanders of regional staffs. Tasks for the RVS: Draw up a plan for municipalities and regions with the following features: 1: Disposition of SDS units, their strengths and composition, disposition of JNA units, their strength and composition. Disposition of storage facilities for weapons and ammunition, mark on the map the ethnic structure by villages, local communes, urban and suburban settlements, in parentheses, Muslim and Croat villages - full green circle. Next to the Croatian villages place the letter H. Serbian villages - blue circle. Mark on the map possible operational modalities for SDS and JNA units and mark this with thin broken lines. 2: Disposition of our units, their strength and composition - potential in the brackets or planned modalities for operations to take place. If necessary, the way in which barracks are to be blocked, how to attack storage facilities for the taking of weapons or merely for blocking them. Mark the positions or locations of these planned facilities for carrying out acts of sabotage, accurately mark the places or regions for municipal logistics bases and regional logistics bases. Plan the areas, villages, and local communes from which the Muslim population will be moved out. Plan the evacuation route, who is to provide security, a place where the population will be received and accommodated. Plan the way in which to secure the federal and republican commodity reserves. 3: Produce this plan on a map and the ratio will be 1:50.000. Use the symbols from the written instructions for the production of maps, and use colours as stipulated in item 1. 4: For the meeting of coordinators and commanders of the RVS, prepare a presentation between 10 and 15 minutes long during which the plan will be presented, problems put forward, and proposals made for solutions, a request of the Main Staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 5: Harmonise plans for regions and produce a defence plan for Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Muslim population. This will be held immediately after the new year. A date will be set at a later stage. 6: In this presentation, special attention must be given to special purpose military industry, the kind of production, and explain our positions and our plan. 7: Review the possibilities of small industry for the production of formation and auxiliary equipment: Bombs, or rather, shells, mines, et cetera, with corresponding documentation. 8: The possibilities of storing and keeping large amounts of weapons and MES. [In English] That's the end of the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Cmeric. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, just for your information, that comes from the book "Cunning Strategy" by Mr. Sefer Halilovic. Have you read that book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The activities that are described in the pages that were read out by Ms. Cmeric on pages 220 and 221, were you aware of any of those planning activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in relation to these aspects of military planning in February 1992, you would tell the Court that you had no awareness of this occurring; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no awareness of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the time of the referendum round about March of 1992, the referendum in relation to the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that created quite some political division, did it not, in your local community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in my town or in my local commune?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your local commune and in your municipality generally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware of a gathering in about April 1992, a gathering in Novi Travnik which was presided over by Franjo Boras, that Croats were discussing with the assistance of Muslims making Kotor Varos an integral part of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware in May 1992 that the three national parties in your local municipality, in an attempt to prevent inter-ethnic clashes, there had been a meeting organised by the Municipal Assembly and the Croat representative, a Mr. Anto Mandic, did not go there, and rather, held a separate meeting with Muslims in the local area, in the handball stadium? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the fact that a public meeting was held at the stadium with members of all the three leading parties in Kotor Varos present: The SDS, the SDA, as well as the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of the killing of Boro Popovic in June of 1992, a Serb? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of, in June 1992, the Crisis Staff of the Kotor Varos municipality, in an attempt to calm inter-ethnic tensions, establishing contact with all the religious leaders of the three religions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of telephone lines going down in the local area in about June 1992, so that telephone contact was lost?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The lines were cut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware in June of 1992 of clashes between Serbs, on the one side, and Croats and Muslims on the other, in villages of Plitska, Bilice, Cirkino Brdo, Cirkici, Hanifici, and Vecici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we please have the names of these villages pronounced properly, because there seem to have been many mistakes made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could invite Ms. Cmeric to read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think that's a very good idea, Your Honour. I think that somehow Ms. Cmeric's pronunciation will be a lot more accomplished than mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have the same problem, all, Witness 144, that we are not native B/C/S speakers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The name of the villages are Plitska, Bilice -- I apologise, then. It must be then -- misprint then. Cirkino Brdo, Cirkici, Hanifici, and Vecici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was aware of what I could see for myself from my own house. I had a view of Bilice, and an elevation where Hanifici is situated. I could see vaguely that houses were being set alight during the night, during the shelling as well as during the day. As for these others, I was not aware of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Witness. Now, were you aware, round about the 24th or 25th of June, 1992, Croat and Muslim representatives calling on -- Croat and Muslim representatives Stipe Maric Sprzo and Muhamed Sadikovic - I hope that pronunciation is adequate - calling on soldiers for negotiations and then organising an ambush in which soldiers were killed and wounded, including Captain Slobodan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just be careful to ensure that the microphones are turned off prior to the witness answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I would indicate that Ms. Cmeric is ably dealing with the microphone at every available opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're referring to the -- in your question you're referring to the part of the video shown yesterday; is that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There seems to be -- that's the aspect that appears to be dealt with there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've referred in your statement to the statement of Mr. Radovan Karadzic in parliament. Do you recall that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that this was broadcast on TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you watch it on TV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the broadcasts of those meetings were of a public nature and usually they were directly broadcast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you listened to the entire speech?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're aware, of course, that when making that statement that you've referred to in your statement, it was immediately followed by "please, I know those are serious words. Serious situations call for serious words. How will you prevent that everybody start killing everybody in Bosnia and Herzegovina?" You recall that bit as well, I take it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he was referring to everybody killing everybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just in relation to this question of what Mr. Karadzic was saying in parliament, you were, of course, aware of the statements that were being made by Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which ones do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, for example, February 27, 1991: "I would sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, but for that peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina I would not sacrifice sovereignty." You recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And statements of that nature, of course, did cause some concern in your local community, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course you are aware that Mr. Izetbegovic stated two years before the war broke out that the Muslims were -- did not yet comprise a big enough majority to make Bosnia a Muslim state? Are you aware of that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of local Serbs in your community being concerned about being a Serb minority within an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they pointed out, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people in your local community disturbed about the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic, on a visit to Turkey in July 1991, asked to join the organisation of Islamic countries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of events in 1993, Witness, were you aware that Serbs from Kotor Varos accepted Croats who in 1993 had been expelled from Travnik by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of Croats leaving -- significant numbers of Croats leaving Kotor Varos on their own request?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to further internal matters in Kotor Varos: Was there in the local politics in terms of the coalition between the HDZ and the SDA felt by the Serbs that the events there were becoming - to your knowledge, of course - politically polarised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no coalition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you tell the Trial Chamber there was no coalition between the Muslims and the Croats in your local area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Not in the political sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the set-up of the Executive Board in your local area, there were I think three Serbs and three non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it the case that SDA and HDZ delegates initiated certain questions during the Assembly sessions without going through the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of Muslims and Croats in your local area arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of paramilitary formations in your local area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of a number of people, a significant number of people, prior to the outbreak of hostilities, people from all three backgrounds - Serb, Croat, and Muslim - wanting to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware of people wanting to leave in the period April, May, June; is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at one of the meetings of the council for national Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond defence, the president of the municipality, who was a Croat by ethnicity, came up with a proposal for Croats to leave Kotor Varos and take their property with them in exchange for which they would be compensated. Following that proposal, the SDS president, Nedjeljko Djekanovic, stated in no uncertain terms as follows: You will not be leaving whenever you see fit, but rather, you will be leaving when we decide, and how we decide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of a meeting with the archbishop of Banja Luka, Bishop Komarica, and the religious Muslim head from Banja Luka, meeting in the Kotor Varos municipality, seeking to find some peaceful outcome? Are you aware of a meeting of that nature around June 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware that there was some discussion about perhaps the possibility of temporarily moving people out so that they could sustain themselves during the period of the conflict? You're not aware of anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of Muslim and Croat paramilitary formations in the directions of Bilice and Kotor? I hope that pronunciation leads you to understand what villages I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I have no idea about that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Mr. Margetts, has the cross-examination raised any wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Judges will have a few questions. First Judge Canivell. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Witness, please, can you tell us during these years 1991, 1992, 1993 you had been speaking about, you had -- you were following what was happening in your town and your village and in the capital town nearby. But at the same time, how did you follow the events in the rest of the country? Through papers, through TV? You did it assiduously, every day? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1991 and 1992, we received information over the media, the television, and the press. I did not, however, watch TV every day. However, there was a free flow of information up until 1992, spring of 1992, when two relays were blocked in Vlasic and Kozara and when we in Kotor Varos were able to cover -- to watch only the programmes aired from Banja Luka and Belgrade. The radio signals which were, however, very poor, did transmit the information from Sarajevo. In part, some of the residents were able to watch TV Zagreb, depending on the range of their antennas. The rest of the information could be gathered from the press, which was mostly from Banja Luka. In 1991, it was Banjalucki Glas. In 1992, it was Srpski Glas. It was renamed. And in part, one could read the press from Belgrade. But, however, in a very restrictive manner from Sarajevo as well. This was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: You said that until the spring of 1992, there was still a free flow of information. What did you mean by that? When you tell us that you had the information coming from different points - Banja Luka, Sarajevo, or even Zagreb - could you precise the sources of this information, in the sense that not the placing from which they were sent; rather, what we would like to know is: I mean the source of the information in the sense of it was the Serbian information, it was Serbian free information, it was Serbian influenced information, it was Croat information, it was Muslim or Bosniak information. Can you precise a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information from Sarajevo originated from the republican TV that was controlled by all the three nationalities in 1991. The information from Belgrade originated from the Serbian national TV, and the same was true for Zagreb, that broadcast the information from the Croatian television. There were no private television channels in 1991. In 1992, having used the relay facilities that we had, we also received information broadcast by the Banja Luka TV. I cannot speak for 1993 because I spent the year in detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: This Banja Luka TV could be considered as a Muslim or, rather, Serbian source of information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be considered as the Serbian source of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I would kindly ask you to clarify several things first. You've said, as far as your experience in detention is concerned, that you established - and this is what you said in English - that there were two factions: There were the Special Forces and the Serbian police force, or the Serbian guards. You've said that the Serbian police was not cruel, that is, it did not mistreat the detainees, but that those who were responsible for that were members of the Special Forces. Is this what you said, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, that is true. We were mostly tortured by members of the Special Forces, by the people wearing camouflage uniforms, under the command of Zdravko Samardzija, and later on, Slobodan Dubocanin. The Serbian police force wore blue uniforms. While we were in detention, they were the guards there. Some of them, like, for instance, Dragan Krejic, who was commander of the camp for a while, used to beat detainees on a daily basis. This is also true for Radenko Keverovic. They, as well as many other guards in the camp, opened the gates to members of the Special Forces and other reserve-force military men to enter the camp and beat the detainees. I will only recount one case here. It happened in August 1992, at the point when I was supposed to be exchanged and returned again to the prison in the school. One evening, members of the Special Forces came in to beat us. I was among the ones who were beaten. A guard at the prison, Popovic, also known as Pop, and known to everyone in Kotor Varos as the waiter Pop, went to the public security station and brought along the inspector Ljubo Petrusic, and following a very long discussion between Petrusic and members of the Special Forces, one could see that they did not have a joint command. Members of the Special Forces went out, only to return an hour later and beat us just as they did earlier on. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Therefore, I can conclude the following: When you say they were mostly beaten by members of the Special Forces, you wish to say that it was more the members of the Special Forces who did that rather than the guards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, this was done by members of the Special Forces, but this was done in the presence of the Serbian police officers in blue uniforms. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Could you establish the membership of these Special Forces, who they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These Special Forces came from Banja Luka, according to what Zdravko Samardzija said, that they came from the security services centre in Banja Luka. I remember very clearly the moment I first encountered Zdravko Samardzija, when I got the pass from him and when I told him that I was a member of the SDA party. He, in turn, told me that this was not an illegal matter, that they had searched our premises, that is, the premises of the SDA party, and that they hadn't found anything that will be in contravention to the Serbian law, unlike the case in Doboj, where they found the, as they called it, the Pastete. When I asked him what it was, he told me it was a type of a land-mine. And I had never heard of that term before, because I wasn't in the army. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] These land-mines were found where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Doboj. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the premises of the SDA party. That is what he said. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] In the premises of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Doboj. This is another town which is -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Fine. I will now change the topic. You have said there's one man, who was a Croat by ethnicity, who was a member of the Assembly, Municipal Assembly, that he had suggested that the Croats leave the area in exchange for a compensation for their property. And then you added that the SDS president, a man by the name of Djekanovic, was against that, was opposed to that. When did this take place, and could the SDS president really do this? Could he have prevented this suggestion from being put into place, and how was it solved in the end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the president of the Assembly, Anto Mandic, came forth with this proposal, because it happened at the end of May in 1992, at the meeting of the council for national defence, when he said the following, "The Croats will not wage any wars in Kotor Varos. Allow us to leave, to take our belongings, to save our lives, in exchange for which you will give us compensation for our property." Djekanovic's reaction was not a calm one. It was a reaction of revolt, because he said, "It is not up to you to decide when you will leave. You will leave when we say so and if we say so, and the way we say." We, however, did not understand fully the meaning of this statement. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And when he said, "This is up to us, we are to decide about this," what did he mean by this? Who was the "we"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant to say that it was up to the SDS to decide about it. A similar statement at the same meeting was given by Savo Tepic, who was the chief of the public security station in Kotor Varos, who said, "Whether Kotor Varos will be part of Republika Srpska is not the point. The point is: Will it be done by force or through peaceful means." The meeting ended in a way that it was concluded that a public meeting should be held in Kotor Varos, in a cinema theatre. But since the interest was quite overwhelming, it was held at a stadium. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. You were talking about late May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And in fact, this meeting was held at a stadium; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held in early June, yes, at the stadium. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And what was the conclusion reached there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting of the council for national defence decided that the SDS should invite their representatives from Banja Luka in order for them to address the citizens of all ethnic backgrounds and explain to them what kind of an advantage would it be for Kotor Varos in joining the Serbian Autonomous District of Banja Luka, that is, the Serbian Republic. The SDS leaders agreed with the idea of them inviting their representatives from Banja Luka; however, on that day when the meeting was scheduled, nobody showed up from Banja Luka. Thus, the presidents of all the parties - the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ - addressed those present and presented the situation in Kotor Varos and put forth suggestions. They were suggesting a peaceful solution. They suggested that peace should be ensured in Kotor Varos - this was suggested by the SDA - and that we should work for the end of the conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to try and reach a peaceful solution as to which body Kotor Varos should belong to. Djekanovic, the SDS president, said that Kotor Varos, in territorial terms, did belong to Banja Luka and that it ought to be part of the Banja Luka region. This was met with general opposition. He was -- then he just left the meeting. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But did it not seem to you that the SDS members from the local area were not in contact? Did it not seem to you that they did not have any contacts with their superiors in Banja Luka? Because it happened, for instance, that they would say something, and then those people in Banja Luka would disagree with it. Were there any contacts between them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were communication contacts between them, because at the meeting of the council for national defence, they did agree to the suggestion that they invite their colleagues from Banja Luka. However, at the public meeting, they said that, due to previous commitments, these certain persons were unable to come. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you for this last answer. You've answered the question concerning the neighbouring village, the one that you lived in, and you said that you yourself came to the conclusion that houses were being set alight during the night, while the villages were being shelled. Did I understand you correctly at the time, or ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did see that the neighbouring villages that I could see from my house, that they were being shelled and that there was fighting going on in the area, and that houses were being set alight, especially during the night, because you could clearly see the fire in the dark. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] We, therefore, came to the conclusion as to why they were set alight, and you even said that they were being torched during the day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Does this mean that they were set alight both during the day and during the night? Did this surprise you at all? Did this take place all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The houses were set alight during the day and during the night, whenever there were clashes on. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I understand that these villages were mostly populated by Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Bilice, there were Croats. In Hanifici, there were Muslims. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I meant to say in Hrvacani. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But there were no Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the suburban areas, in the outlying areas, there were Serbs, meaning in the outlying areas surrounding Kotor Varos. Around Hrvacani, there were several smaller Serb-populated villages, but there were no Serbs in Hrvacani. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You said that houses that came under attack were being torched during the night. It seems to me that if the houses were lit, that this light could serve as a guide to those who were attacking the village and make their job easier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps so. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one or two questions to you, but I first have to inquire whether we'd still have time on the tape. Because otherwise I'd like to finish before the next break. Yes, we still have a couple of minutes. Witness 144, yesterday some questions were put to you in relation to two documents, one being conclusion of the resettlement of Rasim Mehmedovic to Zagreb - you testified you knew him - and the other one was a document in which someone declared that he was voluntarily leaving Kotor Varos municipality for the following reasons, and then stated why he left. You were asked about conditions imposed in order to leave the municipality, and you said you heard about one condition imposed to be voluntarily giving up your property. And we saw on one of these documents that a burned house was given up by that person. I have some difficulties in reconciling conditions imposed and voluntarily giving up. Could you explain exactly what the margin of free will was for those who wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that point, they had no freedom of choice. They could either stay in Kotor Varos or, if they decided to leave, they had to leave their property to the municipality of Kotor Varos. If, for instance, they said that they wanted to leave Kotor Varos, then, if the authorities of Kotor Varos found that they did something that was contrary to the law, they would then be detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What kind of acts contrary to the law would be taken into consideration for detaining those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in prison, a number of detainees were brought in who had registered as wishing to leave Kotor Varos with their families. They would be brought to the prison, whereas the women and children were allowed to leave. From conversations with these people, I learnt that they were being accused of having been opposed to the Serbian authority, that is, of not having been loyal to the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I've got one more question about the relation between the Special Forces and, as I could say, the regular police forces. When you were in detention, did the regular police forces explain to you why you were detained and what the legal basis for your detention was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They never explained this to us, not a single time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it ever asked to them? Did you ever ask: Why do you keep us in detention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked the guards, the guards that we knew from before, the guards that we had once worked with or had been friends with. Their answer, however, was, "We received orders to keep you here. We do not know the reason behind this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my last question is: When regular police forces were present when Special Forces ill-treated detainees, did they ever protest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They never stood up against that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Witness 144. Is there any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have one question that arises from an answer provided to a question from His Honour Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, I'm looking at the clock. Would we still have for one question and answer? Ms. Loukas, would you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's try to finish before we are running out of tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only difficulty is this: I have a document I'd like to present to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do it, then, as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If it could be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This might be a signal that ... Further examination by Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 144, you have before you a decision on the formation of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and it's dated 5 May 1992. Do you recognise the name marked at number 14 of that decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Dubocanin. I recognise that name. He was one of the special unit commanders in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just note that I hadn't ask for an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will give it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P348.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any further questions? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you were asked by His Honour Judge El Mahdi whether you could establish the membership of the Special Forces and who they belonged to, and your answer was that these Special Forces came from Banja Luka. According to what Zdravko Samardzija said, that they came from the security services centre in Banja Luka. Is the membership of the commander Slobodan Dubocanin, of the ARK Crisis Staff, consistent with your observations as to whom these Special Forces belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to that question. That's -- the witness has given his evidence. He's been, Your Honour, cross-examined, he's been asked questions by the Judge. In essence, Mr. Margetts is asking a question that is actually a determination to be made by Your Honours in terms of assessing the evidence. And particularly, to ask it in that leading form, additionally, Your Honour, that question is wholly objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, from the evidence until now, we see the position of Mr. Dubocanin and in the war staff, and we heard extensive testimony on his role. Wouldn't that be sufficient? I mean, consistency ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm satisfied that there's no need for any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that question is then withdrawn. Mr. Margetts, I take it that P348, that the original in B/C/S, only the top part, is tendered into evidence, since only that part is provided in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct. This is just part of a gazette, and accordingly this is the page from the gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So only the upper part, up to where it reads in III.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Witness 144, this concludes your evidence. We'll deal with the documents at a later stage, Mr. Margetts. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Just one matter, Your Honour. The witness has not been present when the summary of his evidence is read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But the summary of his evidence is something which is mainly for the public and not primarily for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, it's to inform the public about the written statement of the witness of which he said that he has reviewed it. So he's aware of it, so we could -- I think we could excuse the witness and then read out the remaining part. But still, of course, we have to see whether there's any agreement finally on what the summary should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think we've reached agreement on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm also a bit concerned about the time and running out of tape. Witness 144, you have come a far way to The Hague. You have answered all the questions put to you by Prosecution, by Defence, and by the Bench. I'd like to thank you very much for coming, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until half past 4.00. And once we start again, we first deal with the exhibits and with the summary. And, Mr. Harmon, I don't know when you had scheduled Mr. Hannis to appear for P202, 203, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He'll be here when we recommence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then we'll deal with these technicalities once we resume, and then I take it the Prosecution is ready to call its next witness. We'll adjourn until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, I take it that we'll receive the newly redacted version of the statement soon, in accordance with the decision given --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- by the Chamber. I do also understand that the parties have agreed on reading out the 89(F) summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, the Chamber wants to express this is not against you or against Ms. Loukas, that, as a rule, we'll read out those statements in the presence of the witness, because that's preferable. It was only under the special circumstances that, well, the witness concluded his testimony and that we would have -- we would have had to ask him to wait for another half an hour for the statement to be read. So therefore, as an exception, we'll now read it in the absence of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the basis for my question was in fact just so the witness was aware of the extent of the evidence that he'd given and that it had come to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the witness could be -- no. We have no English -- we have no B/C/S summaries or -- perhaps you could -- I think that would be proper, if you would -- no, we have no B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness would be still around, of course, we could invite him to, but he may have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness would be still around and if he would prefer to be present, I even would pull the curtains down for that reason, because we really prefer to do that, and perhaps I decided too quickly that we would have a break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't see a need for that because he's accepted your ruling as it was and the reasons for it, and I have advised him of the content of his statement, that I wished to raise it before you [indiscernible] the possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, I think we could proceed. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is the 89(F) summary of Witness 144.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: From late 1990 and throughout 1991, various events in Kotor Varos resulted in disagreements between the SDS and the HDZ and SDA, setting the JNA and the local Serbs against the SDA and the HDZ, including these events: The removal of Territorial Defence weapons by the JNA, the passage of Serbian military convoys through the area, the building of a new military training ground near Maslovare, the mobilisation after the start of the war in Croatia, JNA's seizure of mobilisation lists and records from the local secretariat for national defence, the Serbs' efforts to join Kotor Varos to the Serb-proclaimed Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina. In discussions preceding the removal of weapons, representatives of the HDZ and SDA were threatened by a JNA colonel and by the SDS representatives Slobodan Juric. In October 1991, during the course of discussions in the Municipal Assembly, Nedjeljko Djekanovic, the president of the SDS, threatened the witness, stating, "You have something against the Serbian people. Watch out. Something may happen to you." In the spring of 1991, the witness travelled to Sarajevo with representatives of the SDS, HDZ, and SDA from Kotor Varos to discuss an SDS demand for over 50 per cent of the authority in the Executive Council even though they did not have the majority of seats. In Sarajevo he met with Velibor Ostojic, subsequently the minister for information in the Republika Srpska, and Radovan Karadzic. Ostojic threatened the Muslim and Croat representatives with the use of force. Later, Karadzic joined the meeting, and the SDA candidates felt compelled to accept the solution presented by the SDS in order to maintain the work of the municipal bodies in Kotor Varos. Effectively, there were two political blocks in Kotor Varos: The SDS Serbian block, supporting Slobodan Milosevic's politics, promoting a Serb-dominated Yugoslavia, and the block of the HDZ and SDA opposed to it. From early April 1992, the Serbs declared a new Serbian police force and insisted that the police make declarations of loyalty to the new Serb force. The head of the CSB in Banja Luka, Stojan Zupljanin, attended a meeting in Kotor Varos and was informed that no non-Serb staff wanted to declare loyalty to the Serbs. From around May 1992, checkpoints were set up and movement was restricted around the town. Pursuant to an order from the SDS, there was dismissal of Muslims and Croats from their jobs. In late May 1992, the witness attended a meeting with local SDS officials and two JNA officers from Banja Luka to discuss the issue of Kotor Varos joining the Bosnian Serb Republic. A JNA colonel made it clear that if no agreement could be reached then the incorporation would be carried out by force. The HDZ representative even suggested that the Croats move out, take their belongings and be given a suitable substitute for their property. Nedjeljko Djekanovic told him, "You're not going to move out when you want but when we decide and in the way we decide." The SDS police chief Savo Tepic stated that the question was not whether Kotor Varos would join the Serb Republic but only whether it will be by force or voluntarily. In late May 1992/early June 1992, the SDS took over the municipal building and did not allow non-Serb representatives to enter. Beginning about 11 June 1992, Serb armed forces, including local soldiers, began military action in and around Kotor Varos. On 12 June 1992, the Serbs, Momcilo Komljenovic, president of Executive Council, and Dusko Skoric, together with a special unit dressed in camouflage with insignias, came to the area of town where the witness was. One of the members of the special unit identified himself as Zdravko Samardzija, a lawyer from Banja Luka. Komljenovic stated that the SDS had taken over Kotor Varos and that the town was now considered as part of the Serb Republic. It was also stated that a Serbian Crisis Staff had been formed. They ordered that all weapons be handed over the next day. In late June, firing was directed toward the houses in Cepak and the witness fled to other parts of town, first Sokoline and then to Ravne. On 7 July 1992 the witness was arrested by Serb soldiers and taken to the police station. Between 7 July 1992 and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- And 23 July 1993, the witness was detained overnight, first detained overnight in the police station, then for one and a half months at the Kotor Varos elementary school, and for 11 months in the Kotor Varos prison. On 23 July 1993, he was taken by the ICRC to Karlovac and exchanged. At the police station on 7 July he was interrogated, confined, brutally tortured, and beaten by special unit members under -- Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, the French translation has now finished what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Apologies to Your Honour, and apologies to the translation booth. I will proceed at a more appropriate rate. I'll start this paragraph again. At the police station on 7 July 1992, he was interrogated, confined, brutally tortured, and beaten by special unit members under the command of Samardzija. ARK Crisis Staff member and special police unit commander Slobodan Dubocanin entered the room where the witness was being held and told the witness that unless he gave his interrogators the information that Dubocanin sought, his family would be brought to the police station to be tortured in front of his eyes. Following Dubocanin's appearance, the witness was subject to a game of Russian roulette, witnessed four Cyrillic S's being carved into the back of a fellow detainee and was beaten unconscious. The witness was detained in the elementary school for approximately one and a half months, where he was beaten regularly, forced to perform labour, taken to the front line to dig trenches, and tortured. The following commanders visited the school whilst the witness was detained: Zdravko Pejic, Slobodan Dubocanin, Savo Tepic, Ljubo Petrusic (a police inspector from Zagreb) and Nenad Kajkut. In late August 1992, the witness was transferred to the municipal prison in Kotor Varos. The Special Forces paid regular visits to the prison and beat the prisoners. Prisoners were beaten to death. During 1992, the commanders of the prison, were the former policemen Goran Zaric and Dragan Krejic. They received orders from Zdravko Pejic, Ljubo Petrusic, Savo Tepic, Dragan Bojic, the commander of the Serbian police in Kotor Varos, Slobodan Dubocanin, and Zdravko Samardzija. Zaric told the prisoners that he performed security escorts of convoys that took the non-Serb population across the Vlasic mountain to Travnik. The witness was finally released in July 1993. That concludes the 89(F) summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The speed was perfect, because the interpreters have finished the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have to deal with the exhibits. Madam Registrar, could you assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P324, under seal, pseudonym sheet. P325, under seal, ICTY witness statement dated 18 and 19 December, 1996.
