utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before you turn to D29. Ms. Loukas, you have read the content of this document into the record, and then the witness testified that he didn't know anything about it. Do you insist on tendering D29?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. And I can indicate that we will obtain an official translation and forward that to the Court as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that, if it would be admitted, that we would need an official translation. But I mean, what's the purpose of this being in evidence? I mean, apart from that it was read to the witness, because he ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes, it was read to the witness. The fact is that where that meeting occurred is near that particular municipality. It is a matter of relevance, I would submit, that these events occurred in the circumstances, and I think in terms of the context of the events in the relevant municipality and surrounding areas are important. One looks at the sort of -- the vast bulk of material that comes from the Prosecution on a purely contextual level, Your Honour, and, Your Honour, I submit it's as relevant as the contextual material put forward by the Prosecution in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't object to this extract from that book coming in. We accept the Court's observation that this witness has added nothing to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And effectively, it's been tendered from the Bench. But we don't object to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree that it's rather a dossier piece, I would say, of evidence, rather than anything else. Because otherwise you could read whatever you want to read to a witness and he says, "Well, I don't know anything about." And that document would be in evidence. But I think the parties fairly well understand what it means that this document is then admitted into evidence, that it exists as -- and I also do understand that it's not contested, that it is part of a book, because this is not -- well, this is just explained by Ms. Loukas. So if it's not contested, the Chamber will, I think, accept that it's part of that book of Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to the Prosecution exhibits --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to the Prosecution exhibits, of course, Your Honour, I did register an objection in relation to I think it was 330. That's a document, of course, that contains no signature, no seal, and I asked for further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- information from the Prosecution in relation to the provenance of the document. And just a more general point in relation to the documents put forward by the Prosecution. It is, of course, for the Prosecution to prove their documents. I think it would be important, I would submit, to ensure that when a group of documents are tendered, that the Prosecution indicate how they came into possession of these documents and where they emerge from precisely. I want to make that point of a more general nature. I've made the specific point in relation to the document 330. But I'd like to make that a more general observation in relation to that, that the Prosecution should be providing, in my submission, an indication of where and when the Prosecution came into possession of particular documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way that we had intended to proceed was instead of taking the Court's time with a submission on each and every document, we had intended to only make submissions of that nature in regard to the documents that are contested. Some documents on their face don't admit, in our submission, for a contest, if they have a seal, they're signed, and they're apparently authentic and they're contextualised, then it seems to us to be rather excessive to then also take the Court's time presenting evidence as to the chain of custody and how we came to be in possession of them. So it had been our intention to present these documents. Should there be objections in respect of specific documents, then to call the evidence as those objections arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, now the question is whether we should provisionally admit into evidence that document or to delay. Because it might be that on many documents that we'll hear evidence at the very end. Could the parties perhaps exchange their views on what documents will be contested and that at a later stage we'll deal with all those documents at once, perhaps the first step to be that we receive an explanation by the Prosecution on how they obtained possession of those documents, and if that would not sufficiently resolve the matter, then, if necessary, to even hear witnesses on it. As the parties are aware of the -- the Chamber is not bound by any national rules of evidence and that the authentication of documents might not always follow the -- of what counsel are used to in their domestic practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision on exhibits 330 will be delayed until you have given a response to the objection of Ms. Loukas. I think the first question is where does it come from and the absence of signature and stamps is -- and seals is -- I don't know whether that's the final issue, but if you would first exchange information about that. Then the Chamber will hear whether there's any agreement or whether the objection still stands. And if the objection still stands, we'll then decide on whether or not to admit that document. The Exhibit 325, the Chamber will first receive the -- through the Registry, a new version of the statement and all the other documents are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one further -- there's just one further matter in relation to the exhibits. Ms. Cmeric has pointed out to me that there are some translation issues with a number of the documents. I point out that they are 332, 333, and P338.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So in all likelihood, I assume the best way of dealing with this issue perhaps is for us to date to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- what the issues appear to be in relation to the actual translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the proper procedure would be -- it's a document tendered into evidence by the Prosecution, so they are responsible for an accurate translation. So if you convey to the Prosecution what the problems in relation to the translation are. If the Prosecution, perhaps after having consulted the CLSS, agrees, then we either receive a new translation or the Defence is satisfied that the translation problem doesn't exist any more. So then either replace the translation or do not hear about it any more. I mean, the only thing the Chamber can do is to consult the CLSS as well, so I think it's the proper way to ask the Prosecution to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will consult with Ms. Cmeric and then convey the concerns to CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D29 -- I mean, all the relevant part has been translated into the transcript by the interpreters, so it can be admitted. But D29.1 still has to be received, and then -- of course, it goes without saying that translations are always admitted into evidence unless there's any technical issue. But the admission of D29 is provisional to the extent that the Chamber still has to receive the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Hannis, is it you who will examine the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also did understand that as far as P300 -- no, 200 up to 203, that you still need to consult someone who left the Office of the Prosecution. So we'll hear from that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Elvedin Pasic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, I'd like to ask you to escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Hannis, will there be any 89(F) summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the time scheduled is three hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. May I inquire what time you anticipate the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we started at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We started at 4.30. That means that we -- but we had a late break. 4.30 would mean up to -- I would say a quarter to 6.00 would be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration. I invite you to make that solemn declaration, of which the text is handed out to you now by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I should indicate, Your Honour, this witness has indicated he is preferring to testify in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then I take it that you use the English version of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. Please be seated. May I instruct you that whenever you feel that the use of the English language would cause you any problems, either in listening or in speaking, you're instructed then to address me, because we have simultaneous translation available, and the Chamber would avoid that one single aspect would be missing from your testimony due to language problems. So we leave it up to you to speak English if you want to, but whenever you have a problem, please address me. Mr. Hannis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you again please tell us your name for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My name is Elvedin Pasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how old are you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'm 26 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Pasic, I should tell that you because we're both speaking English, for the benefit of the interpreters, we need to leave a gap between speaking.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'll probably get in trouble more than you will. Would you please tell us where you were born.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village Hrvacani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what municipality and what country was that located?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what municipality in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness an exhibit that's already in. It's the map that's numbered 327.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's not clear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You see the original, so you if can testify on the basis of the original in your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Madam Usher, if it's not clear on the screen, if we have the computer monitor, then we have problems. If you take the computer evidence it becomes more clearly, although even there the letters are difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if you could take a look at the map that's on the ELMO, to your left. I don't know if you can see that any better.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what area that's a map of?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see your village of Hrvacani on the map?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where, approximately, Hrvacani was located in relation to the town of Kotor Varos? Which direction?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: It's to my right, which is west from Kotor Varos, approximately 13 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that 13 kilometres as the crow flies or by road?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: By road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You can set that down for a moment. I want to ask you some more questions about some other villages later, but let me move on for a minute. How big was your village? How many houses in Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Approximately a hundred houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the people who lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: All Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see on the map that two nearby villages to Hrvacani are Tepici and -- to the north and Savici to the east. What was the ethnicity of those villages?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also on the map, further south from your village, there is a village named Dabovci. In 1992 did you have any relatives living in that village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My sister, who was married at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what her husband's name was?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Elvir Lihovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who in your family lived with you in Hrvacani in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I lived with my mom, my father, and later my brother who joined me when he came back from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he doing in Belgrade in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Right before the war, my brother, after high school, went to Belgrade to join JNA, and he was accepted at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in May of 1992, as I do my math, you would have been 13 going on 14 years of age; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you attending school then?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I went to Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of school was that? Did students of all three ethnic groups - Croats, Serbs, and Muslims - attend that school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May of 1992, shortly before your 14th birthday, did you notice any unusual activity in the neighbourhood of your village and your school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Judges about what that was.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Sure. In May 1992, right before the holiday, Muslim holiday Bajram, we noticed that our neighbours from Tepici and Savici were digging trenches from both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Our two well-known men at that time named Muho Dugonjic and his brother Murat Dugonjic, with the concern seeing our neighbours digging trenches, decided to go and talk to our neighbours in a place in between -- there was an elementary school between Hrvacani and Savici, where I attended my four grades. Asked our neighbours why they were digging trenches around the village, and they told them that this is nothing to worry about. It's just a military exercise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before this event in May 1992, in prior years, had you seen military exercises in your part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was attending my school, actually, the end of the 7th grade, one day I was outside taking a break in between classes, 15-minute break. This was the first time when I noticed a big convoy of JNA tanks and armed vehicles going from direction Kotor Varos, passing Vrbanjci. I was with my friends across the street, and we couldn't cross the street right away because of the armed vehicles passing by. We were greeted by the soldiers with a sign -- this sign, and they were passing by. As soon as they passed by we went back to school. We were nervous. We asked our teachers what is going on and they didn't answer the questions. Nobody knew. At that time, we noticed that something is going to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop there for a second. You indicated a sign and you held up -- you held up your thumb and the first two fingers, as I'm doing now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did that sign mean to you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: To me, at that time, we knew that there were a sign of JNA at that time. I don't know exactly what that meant, but it meant that -- we learned from our fathers that they were actually using the sign for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to this year of 1992, had you seen other military exercises by the JNA in your area, in previous years, in 1991 or 1990?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember as a little boy, in the past, that they used to have exercise, and as a matter of fact, they were -- one day I remember they had exercise in our village with the regular JNA uniforms, olive-green, and I remember it was -- as a little boy, it was kind of fun for us to join them, and they were carrying weapons, but not real. And they were more like playing, and it was exercise. I remember we had fun with, you know, they let us go with them and, you know, touch the gun and play. But this time it was totally different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on those previous occasions, had anyone ever dug trenches around their villages in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you seen tanks during the previous exercises in the earlier years?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you said that you saw your neighbours in the Serb villages of Tepici and Savici digging trenches around the time of the Bajram holiday in 1992. Do you remember approximately what date that was, or can you relate it to your birthday of June the 3rd? Was it before or after that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't really remember it, but I know it was May, and it was really nice outside. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about this time, do you recall an incident where some Serb soldiers came to your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges about how that happened and what they did.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Approximately four or five days before holiday Bajram, we had five, six armed -- well-armed soldiers in camouflage uniform walked through our village from south side of the village and through the village. I remember I was outside playing with my friends when we saw the soldiers coming. Because my house was faced south towards Dabovci and Vrbanjci and we could clearly see the road and people coming and going. When we saw them, my mom -- we wanted to run. We -- as a kid, wanted to run and, you know, join them. I remember my mom was telling me, "Don't go. Don't go, because they might come in and get your brother." And she put me in a room, and as a little kid, I didn't want to wait. I escaped and rang on the back side of a house, and I knew that they were going to cross the road right in the middle of the village, and I knew that I can meet them there. So we went, me and my friends, to see who is coming. And right at this crossroad that was in the middle of the village, we had a place that people hang out at night, you know, sit around and talk. We were waiting there with an old man who was sitting there every day, and these soldiers, they came in and, and as they were coming, they were -- they had bullets crossed. They were fully armed. And they greeted us. They were saying good day, and good morning. And they were just saying that this is a nice village. Some of my friends and people later on knew. One of them -- I noticed one of them, who was Boro. I don't recall his last name, but I know him. I've seen him. He was a neighbour. And my mom later on told me that they were all neighbours from Tepici and Savici. We also found out later on that when we escaped to Vakufci, that this was a bet made between them that they can -- they're going to walk through Hrvacani fully armed and see if somebody is going to stop them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anything happen other than they walked through the village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No. They were just pointing at houses. I remember the house of Muho Dugonjic, who was a well-known rich man, huge house, just finished, it was enormous, and he -- one of the soldiers turned around and he said, "Is that a hotel?" And we were saying no. He says, "Wow, that's a nice house." And they were all staring at the houses and a mosque. No -- nothing. They just walk through the village and continue walking towards Savici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you describe the houses in your village compared to the houses in some of the neighbouring villages? I mean, how did your village compare economically or in terms of prosperity with neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Well, our -- we -- our village had a lot of people working outside of Bosnia and especially in Germany, Austria, and our village was considered as a really rich economically. Houses, really nice houses, big houses. We had telephones. Everything that can, you know, man can ask for. I remember when they were ready to build the road with asphalt through the village and we asked our neighbours, Tepici and Savici, to join us, to get money so we can share the road. We always did share before that. But to make it easier instead of having just a regular road. I remember they refused, so we stopped with asphalt half a distance, and Tepici and Savici didn't want to cooperate. So in my mind, I think we were really a strong village at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after this event where the Serb soldiers walked through your village during the Bajram holidays, did anything unusual happen with regard to your neighbours in Savici and Tepici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Around the time this happened, or shortly after this event where the Serb soldiers walked through your village, did anything unusual happen to your village in connection with those neighbouring Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the next thing of importance or the next thing that was out of the ordinary that happened in your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Okay. Second day of Bajram. The tradition, our tradition is families celebrate Bajram by going around and visiting families, friends, and eating every day. As a little boy, I was running around, and on south side of our village, looking at Dabovci, we noticed on Novakovo Brdo two tanks and approximately 15 to 20 soldiers in the distance pulling out of woods, going in and out. I immediately -- when we saw that, I immediately informed my cousin, Akif, who was walking with the men from the house, to the house, that something is going on in our south side of the village, towards Novakovo Brdo. And soon he joined me and we find out that there were two tanks right on Novakovo Brdo and some soldiers. They were -- they had uniforms, olive-green uniforms and, like I said, 15 to 20 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what Novakovo Brdo is. Is that a town, a village, or what?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Novakovo Brdo is a hill, right above Dabovci. It's connected actually to Dabovci but it's a hill, south side -- south from my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you told your cousin Akif about this activity?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Akif and a lot of men, men who were walking from the house, to the house, joined with hodza, gathered together, and it happened to be right next to my house that they were passing by. So they decided to go in my house, to sit down and discuss this issue that was going on with our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to me who or what is hodza.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Hodza is a -- he was in charge of mosque. He represents our -- he's imam who greets families, especially during the holidays, going from house to house, joining the families, and he was in charge of praying and calling people around to pray.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the men discussed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember that they were saying something about that the war is on our door and that they need to sit down and discuss how many weapons there is in the village, and that they gathered in a -- we had a huge house. In the house, approximately 20 men, including my father, and I wanted to get in, but at that time he told my mom that we need to stay out of this, and he closed the door. And I don't know what happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there was any call or demand or request for the people, the men in your village to surrender weapons before this date?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did the men meet and discuss things that you weren't allowed to sit in and hear about?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Approximately 30 minutes, an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that meeting finished?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: The meeting finished. Everyone went separate directions. My father told us to stay in the house and just to stay safe, because he wants to go outside and see clearly that something's going to happen that night, and he just left the house that night. I don't know where he went. But we stayed in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anything happen that night?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Approximately around 11.00 that night, bombing and shelling started and lasted all night, until morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you and your mom do when --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you tell us what you and your mom did when the bombing and shelling started.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We joined our -- my aunt and my cousins. We gathered all together. Because my aunt was -- her house was south from my house, really close. My village was kind of expanding at that time and she was close to Vrbanjci. She asked my mom if she can join us that night because electricity went off. And I forgot to mention that also that night, before shelling started, my cousin Akif came over to call his sister, who was at Vrbanjci at that time, and he was trying to reach -- he finally reached her on the telephone, and she told him that three tanks took positions in Vrbanjci and that she was really afraid. And she asked him what is going on. And at that time, he wanted to call -- we asked him to call my sister, who was married -- who was at Dabovci. He was trying so hard to reach her, but everything was -- he was trying so hard. So many voices at that time, he could not reach her at all. At one point I remember him saying, "Okay. I want to introduce myself. I want to reach this person. Is there any chance that I can -- we can somehow introduce ourselves so I can reach this person?" And they were -- they -- he told us - we were sitting right next to him - that they just laughed at him, and soon afterward telephone lines were cut off, and electricity. So go back to my aunt. She asked my mom to come back and spend the night, that night with us, and we went to -- into a house, our neighbour house who was -- they had a room kind of going into the ground, hidden room, and we found out that's the best place to stay that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the next morning, did the bombing and shelling stop?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember we were all together. It was just terrible that night. It was just shelling everywhere. Serbs used megaphone and announced that -- I remember that that was one of the terrifying scenes, hearing the voices on the megaphones calling and saying: "Balija, boil the coffee," calling Muho's and Murat's name. "Have baklava and halva ready for us. Soon we will come and dance kolo." That was -- we were really scared when we heard that. Laughing, bombing and shelling lasted all night. And I remember early in the morning somebody broke the window, and it was my dad and he told us, "Get out. Get out. You're the last group in the village. Serbs are taking over." As a matter of fact, our neighbour house is in flames because it was hit by something, by bombing. And he told us that they were coming from the north side, from Tepici, and they were already in the houses and burning houses. At that time, it was just a chaos. We tried to follow him. He says, "Just get out." Number one, we couldn't get out of doors because we were faced, Novakovo Brdo, and they were shooting at us all the time. So we had to crawl through the window and go behind the houses, run one by one in a gaps that there was open area. And I remember for the first time after all this, I saw my brother, who was waiting on the one -- there was a road coming in our village, and he told us, "I want you to stay and listen to me carefully. We got a sniper hitting and shooting this area, and I want you to cross it quick as you can, one by one, and don't run on the street. Just cross it and get down and just try -- stay cover." I remember I was holding this little boy. His mom was pregnant, and she was carrying small -- a little baby. And she told me, "Grab him. Don't pay attention, if you pull his arm, if he's hurt, if he's crying, just grab him and don't let him go." We crossed that road, and they were firing at us all the time. This woman, she couldn't run because she just had a baby. I remember we got down into a -- we crossed the road. She was standing. We were all shaking. She had holes between her legs from bullets. But thank God nothing hit her. That was really scary. We joined a group -- we joined a group of people who were older people trying to catch up with the group. Already people were left and going towards Plitska, which was mainly Croats. As a matter of fact, all the Croat people living there, they offered us to come and just escape from Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second and ask you a few specific questions. Approximately how far was Plitska from your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Approximately three to four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people did you see in your group? How many villagers were trying to get out of the village and go toward Plitska?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Like I mentioned, I was -- our group of five families, six families, were the last ones leaving the village, and I heard that most of the villagers left except five to six people, elderly people who couldn't -- decided to stay in the village, but they couldn't move. Mainly everyone left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later find out what happened to the elder people who stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They all got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you found out about that when you returned to your village sometime later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll talk more about that later on. I want to kind of go in sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a quarter to 6.00. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we broke, sir, you were telling us about leaving your village and going towards Plitska. After you had crossed the road where you were told there were snipers, did you have to go through any additional hazards before getting to Plitska?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us about that briefly.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Right in between Hrvacani and Plitska, there was a field, open field. Approximately 300 to 500 metres up the hill, we had to crawl to get into a wooden area. That area was -- we were -- they were shooting at us from Novakovo Brdo and Tepici. We had to crawl there to Plitska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Plitska, was your mom also there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. My mom -- finally joined my mom after we got a little separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about your dad and your brother? Do you know where they were at this time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My father, we got to Plitska together to join my mom. I haven't seen my brother until later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Plitska, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Approximately two to three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We went to Cirkino Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that another village in the area?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of Cirkino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Cirkino Brdo was all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you decide -- or how did you happen to go to Cirkino Brdo at this time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we got to Plitska, local people gave us weekend houses to stay in them. When a guy name Hasan - I don't recall his last name - from Cirkino Brdo came to pick up his sister Zena, who was my aunt, to take her to Cirkino Brdo, that's when we joined Zena. And he came there with his tractor and he took us to Cirkino Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who went with you personally? You and who else from your family went?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I went with my mom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how long did you stay in Cirkino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many days, but I know that Hasan told us later on that Serbs came to -- at that time, Cirkino Brdo signed loyalty to Serbs, and one day he came in and he told us that Serbs told him if he continues to feed balijas from Hrvacani, that his family and others are going to get killed. That's when he told us and we left Cirkino Brdo, because we didn't want to cause any problems to the other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "we left," do you mean you and your mom or any other people?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I left with my mom and other people who were in the area, but I don't know how many of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other people, were they also people from your village of Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they -- and these other villagers, were they military-aged men, children, or what?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Just the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go from Cirkino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We went to Bilice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is Bilice also a village in Kotor Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of that village, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the people there take you in, take you and your group of fellow villagers from Hrvacani in?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if it was days or weeks or --

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I know it was weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There came a time when you left there, then?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we got to Bilice, I remember we entered the side where 15 to 20 well-armed soldiers, mainly Croats, were waiting for us. They knew that we were coming in. And they offered us houses and food to stay in, with the local ones. We worked in the fields and stayed there. I don't know how many -- it wasn't days, it was weeks, until the food was running low, and we decided to move out of Bilice to Hrvacani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to your original home village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that Cirkino Brdo had signed loyalty to the Serbs. I take it based on your description of the armed men in Bilice, that they had not signed loyalty to the Serbs at that time.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you decided to go back to your home village from Bilice?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Approximately 50 to 70 women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how far it was between those two points?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Between Bilice and Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I would say five to six kilometres, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way there, did you meet any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We met two soldiers close to our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: They were two Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone in your group know them or know where they were from?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Well, the area we met them was before war, three Serb houses in between Plitska and Hrvacani. One of the guy -- we were getting tired of, like I mentioned before, living and food was running low. We decided to go back to Hrvacani and then we met them. And one of them was -- I guess he was hurt, because he was -- the other guy was carrying him, and he was holding his stomach like this. And when they saw us, they were surprised, and they told us that -- one of them got really angry and says, "What are you balijas doing here?" And my mom and this other woman, Razija Dugonjic, said, "We want to go back to our village because there's no other place for us to go." He says, "There is no place for you guys to go other than Turkey. You belong to Turkey. And I don't care if you get killed." And then they left towards Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your group go on then to your home village of Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We passed three houses and we entered our village from south side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell the Court what you saw when you arrived there. What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we entered the village from south side, the place was totally destroyed. I remember my aunt had a house, like I mentioned before, was brand new house, totally burned, destroyed, cattles were all loose, some of them killed on the road. Then later on we find out that all the houses were damaged, burned, totally looted and destroyed. But three houses who were newly constructed were still remaining still.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this time did you find anything -- find out anything about the old people who had stayed behind when you all went to Plitska?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. When we reached the crossroad in the middle of village, we got separated. Everyone was running to their home. I remember I went with my mom to check our house. We walked through the burns and destroyed houses and we got to our house. Just the four walls left and two chimneys totally burned. Everything in the house was looted. Nothing left. I found out my dog was killed, and we didn't want to stay long because we got really nervous and scared. So I remember I got some apples from the tree, and my mom called me and said, "Let's go. Let's go meet others." We went to this crossroad when we found this woman crying and -- crying and yelling. Then they found this old man, Dugonjic Ibro, who was really religious man and didn't want to go at that time when we left the village. He was killed and burned. They found his bones and they were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take your time. If you want a break or a Kleenex, there's one right there. Whatever you need.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My mom told me to stay there. They took his bones and they buried him. Also, the rest of the remaining families went and looked to find if there is anything left. They found four other elder people who were also killed. They gathered the bones and we buried them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in your village? I'm sorry. Was there a mosque in your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: The mosque was no longer standing. The minaret was destroyed. And I wanted to go up there because I remember as a little kid I used to go up there. And I wanted to go steps and my mom told me -- somebody mentioned, "Don't go. Might be mines or something up there." So I didn't want to actually -- I wanted to go, but I didn't want -- they didn't let me to go. But minaret was totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have the next --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could we have the next photograph given a number and shown to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need to put off your microphone, since we have no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I forgot, Your Honour. I'll leave it on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P349.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, can you tell us if you recognise what's in that picture.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: This is remaining of dzamija in Hrvacani. There is no -- you can see there is no minaret here, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out from anyone about how the mosque had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We found out that it was destroyed with explosive, because during the time when they were shelling our village, when we left the minaret and dzamija was still standing. And the people -- there was one family who actually wanted to -- stayed there, and they told us when we came back, when we were coming back, they were -- and they were surprised at seeing us. Then later on they told us that it was destroyed by explosive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were these people that told you about that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: An old man who stayed with his wife. He was -- lived close to the dzamija. He didn't want to go anywhere, and he was at that time, he was still alive, but later on we found out that they killed him too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he -- did he say -- did he tell who had done the mining of the mosque, set the explosives?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: He said that local ones did from Tepici and Savici. He did not mention the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you all were there in the village and after you had each looked at your homes, did anyone come and speak with you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Soon after we all gathered and buried the killed ones, we saw tractor full of soldiers coming from Tepici towards village. Then we all gathered together. We knew that they were coming in. And soon, five minutes later, tractor pulled off and 15 to 20 soldiers got out and some of them had camouflage uniforms, some of them olive-greens, and also some of them had covered faces. One of them was really vicious to us. He started yelling and saying, "What are you balijas doing here? There's no place for you." And there was this one soldier who was really kind, who sustained him and tried to calm him, and asked us nicely: What are we doing here? And we told him we are coming back, there is no place for us but the home. And also I remember we had a little -- we had one pregnant woman with us who was ready to deliver a baby and she needed water so bad. When we were asking for the water and this soldier told us to stay there and he'll send somebody to get us from Tepici. And 15 minutes later they got us a bucket of water. And he asked us, "Why do you want to stay here?" And like I mentioned that we decided to stay. And he says, "Well, there is nothing here. Everything is destroyed." And at that time my mom says, "Is there any chance that we can go to Garici and Vakufci, to our relatives?" And he says, "That's a better idea than stay here." But five to six families decided to stay there because they didn't have anybody, no relatives in Vakufci and Garici. Then he offered us two soldiers, whoever wanted to go, we left there for Garici and Vakufci, and like I mentioned, five to six families stayed there that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers who came from the direction of Tepici, did your mom or anyone know any of them? Were they locals or were they Serbs from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I did not recognise anybody. My mom says they were all locals. Some of them from Tepici and some of them from Savici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where is Garici generally in relation to your home village of Hrvacani? What direction, and approximately how far, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Vakufci is to our left, east side from Hrvacani, it goes Savici, then Hrvacani, then Garici. I don't remember how far away from Hrvacani. Approximately a kilometre, one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of those two villages?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: All Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to go through any Serb village to get to Garici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: In order to get to Vakufci and Garici, we had to cross Savici, which was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to your group on your way to Garici when you went through Savici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we got to Savici, there were civilians waiting for us, and I remember this one woman was really angry and really vicious to us. My mom knew her name, and later on her son, Dalibor, was going to school with me. She was really angry. She wanted to shoot us. She was actually going for the gun from this soldier. And asked us, "What are you balijas doing here, moving around while our soldiers are dying at Vecici." And she -- this soldier pushed her and told us just to move on, to start walking. She started spitting on us and throwing stones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many of you were in this group that went from your old village to Garici, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Approximately 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Garici once you got there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: In order to get to Garici we had to cross Vakufci. Some families stayed there, but we went straight to Garici because we had our relative, Atif Agambegovic, who wanted us to come there. And we stayed at Garici approximately three to four weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you decide to leave Garici after three to four weeks?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Once again, food was running low. We helped, everywhere we go, we helped people around to work on the fields, get some food. But nobody expected this, and food was really running low. So we decided to go back to Bilice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived back at Bilice, what was happening in that village at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw my brother, he insisted for us to come to Bilice. He was waiting for us and told us that somehow he got information that Bilice would not hold out for a long time and that he gave us the option to go to Vecici with him or go back to Garici, which he insisted us to go back to Garici because it was getting dangerous. He gave us 200 Deutschmarks, and we noticed local ones packing and at that time we knew that something is going to happen. So we didn't want to waste and we came back again to Garici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This second time that you were at Bilice, approximately how long did you stay?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Four to five days. I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you saw locals packing. What do you mean by that? What were they doing exactly?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: They were packing their belongings. And we asked -- because this lady who gave us a house to stay in, we asked her, "Why are you packing?" And she said, "We are going for Travnik. We have to leave. We have to pack." And at that time, we -- people got -- it was just a chaos. We didn't know where to go. But they were packing just their belongings to get out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went back to Garici for a second time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later hear about what happened to Bilice? Did it indeed fall?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We heard that pope [phoen] cooperated with the Serbs, signed -- or made an agreement for all the people living in Bilice that they're going to -- Serbs offer them safe passage to Travnik as long as they give up their weapons. And anyone who -- everyone who was in the Bilice at that time did survive. Anyone who didn't want to stay, left to other places, Vecici, Garici, Vakufci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Garici this second time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Approximately one to two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you come to leave Garici after this second stay there? What happened?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember we were outside every night. Electricity was cut off. It would come on and off sometimes a day and night. We were sitting outside and watching sporadic firing at Vecici. When our cousin, Akif Pasic, came in from somewhere and just jumped in the house and said, "Okay. Let's have a coffee," and we got really scared because he looked really terrible at that time, long hair, beard, and he was armed. My mom asked him, "What are you doing here?" He says, "Well, I'm here to drink coffee with my friends." And she was, like, "What do you mean?" He says, "Well, I got two Serb friends waiting for me outside." So indeed, there were two soldiers waiting for him outside. He says, "I'm here to tell you that tomorrow civilians from Hrvacani, you need to pack and go. We made an agreement with the Serbs for you to go to Vrbanjci, get a travel document, and all of you need to go to Vecici." [Realtime transcript read in error "Hrvacani"] He didn't stay for long, five minutes he drank, and then he left with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these two soldiers that were accompanying him, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs, well-armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it surprise you to see your cousin, who was armed, to be with two armed Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We were really surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I just ask one thing which is a bit unclear in the transcript to me. When you told us about an agreement that was made with the Serbs for you to go to Vrbanjci and get a travel document and all of you need then to go to -- and what did you then mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vecici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Vecici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have the next document. It is entitled "Extraordinary Session of the War Presidency continued." The English is 03005024. If that could be given a number and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution exhibit number P350.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I want to refer you to the last paragraph in that document, which is dated the 2nd of November, 1992. And if I may, I'll just read that. It says: "In the further course of the session, Captain Balaban brought representatives of Vecici to negotiate, namely, Raif Alagic, and Pasic, to whom Colonel Bogojevic conveyed the position of the command and then asked them how much time they needed to hand over their arms and sent them back to Vecici to come back with an answer." Do you know if the Pasic referred to in that paragraph in that document would be your cousin who was involved in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But I know that night he came in with the two Serb soldiers, so I assume he was. Otherwise, why would he come with two soldiers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know approximately -- not the specific day, but in relation to the time when your cousin came and told you about this, how much later was it that Vecici actually fell?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I would say six to seven days, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the next day after Akif had came -- had come and told you about this, did you go to Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, with my mom and all the people from Garici and Vakufci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many of you were in that group?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I would say approximately 50 to 70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any military-aged men?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, sir. All civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do in Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we got to Vrbanjci, they told us to stay in front of old school - I remember that school - until somebody goes in the new school to get a travel document. At that time, I was -- we were on the grass, sitting on the grass, and a lot of soldiers were passing by, when one of the soldiers approached my mom and told her, "What are you doing here?" And he was -- my mom told me that he was Josip. She knew him at that time. She knew him from the past. He asked her, "What are you doing here? And how is everything?" And my mom just responded, "We're fine. We're okay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: He was Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything to your mom or your group about going to Vecici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything to us, but five minutes later, whoever came from our group went and got the document, came back, and they told us to get up and move on slowly towards Vecici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get to Vecici from Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We had to talk from Vrbanjci all the way to Vecici, slowly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you got there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember when we were crossing and going on the road and crossing -- we crossed the bridge, after the bridge there was a road all blocked with the trees. We had a hard time to cross it. And as soon as we approached it to Vecici, we found a man coming out of bushes, approximately 15 to 20 of them, well armed, waiting for us, and told us to go in two different groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time, who were the people in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: All Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Croats?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- how big a village was Vecici, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Vecici was a big village, because they had two dzamijas in the village. I remember when we approached the village, they -- somebody told us, me and my mom, that we have to go on right-hand side from the Cvrcka River that was dividing village on two sides. So we joined -- we went right-hand side, and as we were passing by, I seen a lot of houses. It's a big village, but I don't know how big. I mean, they had two mosques.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what condition was the village in, or the buildings in the village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Everything pretty much was destroyed. I remember when we were walking, at that time, my father joined us and he told us, "Okay. Follow me." Because he knew some friend who is going to give us a place to stay. And we were walking by, and these first 30 houses that we passed by were completely burned. And we know why: Because when I was in Cirkino Brdo, Serbs used the air strike for three days to attack Vecici. And I remember the one third day when we were outside watching bombing, Serb soldiers from this side of Croat village next to the Vecici approached. There was a clear open area and we could have seen -- we easily saw and some of us used binoculars. They entered the village and they broke the line. They got there and they burned 30 houses and killed everyone who was in there. And even our hospital that we know, because my aunt -- my cousin was in the hospital, and he survived from that hospital because he crawled and just -- into a ditch when they came in to kill everybody. And he was telling us how everything went -- run out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you a few questions to clarify it for me. You talked about seeing air strikes for three days on Vecici. When had you seen that happen?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Like I mentioned that we were at Cirkino Brdo, me and my mom, working on the fields and Hasan's house. And one day we were working on the fields and aeroplane was really -- coming really low, and we thought: This is it. We did not know what's going to happen. So we were just -- my mom, I heard my mom saying, "Just lay down and cover your head." They came in and they were attacking from -- coming from Cirkino Brdo and shooting at Vecici, for three days, during the day only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were at Cirkino Brdo right after you left Plitska, when you first left your home village; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't come to Vecici village yourself until some months later; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In showing you around the village, did your father indicate that some of this damage had been it done by aerial bombing?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Like I mentioned, we -- somehow they got -- Vecici got agreement with Serbs for five days, no fighting, for five days, no fighting, no nothing. So the following morning, my father took me out and he says, "I want you -- I want to walk -- I want to show you some, you know, places where I've been." And he took me out. And the first weekend house that he was living in at the time, he says there was a big old tree in front of it. I remember I was walking by and he says, "Look at this tree." And big, big bomb was laying right next to it. I guess unactivated. Hit the tree and it felt like somebody just used a saw and cut it off. He was in the house, and when they woke up they find out that it didn't explode or anything. And he says, "Don't come near it, because we don't know what is this." And then he took me -- we were passing by mosque, and this one house that I asked him, "What is that, Dad?" And they had three or four graves freshly in front of the house. And he says, "This whole family got killed from air strikes. A bomb dropped on the house and burned them all." So they buried them right in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say anything about the burning bomb?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: He says that according to him, they used napalm bombs, because when they explode, everything was on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The unexploded bomb you saw where the tree had been sheared off, how big was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember I was -- at that time I was 14 years old, so it was my -- approximately my size. It was big, big.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You seem pretty tall to me. How tall were you when you were 14 years old?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I know the bomb was this big.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You're holding your hand out indicating a height of maybe a foot higher than the desk you're sitting at.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: And this round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you're indicating with your hands how many metres or inches would you say that is?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a metre or two. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, how long did you stay in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, for the record, I think the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- indicated approximately a height of one metre and 40 centimetres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Four to five days. I don't really remember, but I think it was four to five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was happening in Vecici during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: The fifth day, the bombing and shelling started, and soon we were told that we have to go in cellar. And the people we -- in the house, they said, "Okay. We have to go outside." And right next to the house there was a cellar. We have to go in there and the fighting started again. Firing, bombing. I think it was the fifth day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you decide to leave?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember that night my father came, and he was -- he came over to say goodbye to me and Mom, and he did. He came in and he hugged me and he told my mom, "We're going to leave tonight. And I don't know if I should take everything with me or if -- you know, I leave him, I'm afraid if we leave him with you," we heard that Serbs were taking all the boys from convoys in Banja Luka. "So I think he's better off if he goes with me." And at that time my mom says, "I think it's a good idea if he goes and joins you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was your father leaving with? Was he going by himself or was he going with a group?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We left at night with a group of 500 to 700 people, total, mainly men. I would say three females and approximately 15 boys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what age were the boys? Your age?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the rest of the people that were in Vecici? Were there -- well, obviously you told us about your mom. Were there other women and younger children in the village as well?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they going to do?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember my mom asking my dad, "So what are we going to do if you guys are leaving? What are we going to do?" He says, "Tomorrow you all raise the flag, white flag, find something, white shirt or something, and just march towards Vrbanjci."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a good point for me to stop, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pasic, we'll conclude for today. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, a quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon [Realtime transcript read in error "morning"]. Madam Registrar, this same courtroom? Yes. I give notice to the parties that on Friday we are sitting in Courtroom II. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Pasic out of the courtroom. May I instruct you, Mr. Pasic, not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and you're still about to give tomorrow and the days that may follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the transcript says -- you said a quarter past 2.00 in the morning. I assume you mean 2.00 in the afternoon tomorrow

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I meant a quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. I did not know what I said. But I said it wrongly, I do understand. Mr. Pasic, it's understood that you're expected at 2.15 in the afternoon and not any earlier. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Pasic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just could you tell us whether you're approximately on schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I think I'll be done in an hour or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Pasic was scheduled for three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, would there be any problem to start or even to cross-examine the witness tomorrow, once Mr. Hannis has finished?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour. And I would have thought that the witness's evidence would be completed tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thursday. So that leaves the question of what we're going to do in relation to Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be my next question, yes, under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I don't know if that was previewed to Your Honours, but we have no other witnesses after this witness this week. I apologise to the Court for not being able to use that time with the witness tomorrow. This was partly -- this was a week that we had Ms. Hansen scheduled and then when we moved her, it was difficult to find a good fit. And this witness we did not want to keep over because he came from across the ocean. And we didn't want to have to continue him over to the following week, when Monday is a holiday and we have a summons witness on Tuesday, the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand, Mr. Hannis. I make two observations. First of all, that Prosecution still has to get used to its own higher speed; and second, that what the Defence doesn't get from the Chamber, it gets it from the Prosecution. That means some additional time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's just one matter I'd like to mention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If it does appear that we won't be sitting on Friday, I must say from the Defence perspective, all is not lost, because there are in fact some Association of Defence Council training programmes on the EDS system, the electronic disclosure system, CaseMap, LiveNote, that all members of the Defence team were hoping to attend. So there may be a silver lining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As every cloud has. Then most likely we'll not sit on Friday. If there's any time left tomorrow, that might be possible, then I'd like very much to continue reading into the transcript of 92 bis statements. We have still a few left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have a number of those ready that we can read in tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think maybe there's still a few exhibits from prior witnesses that I'd like to move from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- from prior witnesses. Of course we have still a list of -- a limited list, but on that list is also numbers 200 until 203. But it might be that if we have no information yet, you expected it to arrive only on Friday that we might deal with the remaining exhibits to give decisions on that if any time is left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had specifically in mind the witness Mr. Medanovic, who testified on the 5th of October. He was the gentleman from Kljuc. And I think there were only four or five exhibits, 308 through 312.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll check that. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
